model.label: Statutory social health insurance through competing sickness funds, with an opt-out private tier

overview.statement: In 2024 about 89% of residents had statutory health insurance and about 10% substitutive private insurance; others had other forms of cover, leaving roughly 0.1% uninsured.
The multi-payer statutory system runs through 96 sickness funds, financed by wage-related contributions shared by employees and employers plus federal subsidies.
A self-governing body of payers and providers, the Federal Joint Committee (G-BA), decides which technologies, medicines and devices the statutory benefit package covers and sets care standards.
Every resident must hold health insurance, either in the statutory system or through a substitutive private plan.
Health insurance has been compulsory in Germany since January 2009.

financing.statement: Contributions are pooled in a central health fund and reallocated to the sickness funds by risk adjustment. The general rate is 14.6% of gross income, plus a fund-specific supplementary rate that averaged 1.7% in 2024; employers and employees split both equally.
The health ministry set the average supplementary contribution for 2027 at 2.9%, unchanged from 2026; each sickness fund still sets its own rate.
Employees earning EUR 73,800 a year or more, the self-employed and civil servants may stay in the statutory system or switch to private insurance.
Private insurance premiums are set by age and health risk, whereas statutory contributions depend on income.
Mandatory long-term care insurance, introduced in 1994, covers almost the entire population, with contributions split between members and employers.

covered.statement: The statutory benefit package is broad and identical for every insured person, going beyond essential services; substitutive private plans usually match or exceed it.
Patients may freely choose physicians, psychotherapists, dentists, pharmacists and urgent care services; GPs are often the first point of contact but are not formal gatekeepers.
Since 2004 sickness funds have had to offer an optional GP-centred care model, and some reward members who follow it.
For medicines approved in the EU in 2020-2023, Germany had the EU's shortest average wait for reimbursement: 128 days, against an EU average of 578.
As of January 2025, 90% of authorised medicines were reimbursed in Germany, the highest share in the EU and about twice the EU average of 43%.

Since the AMNOG law took effect on 1 January 2011, a manufacturer must submit a dossier on a new medicine's benefit at launch, and the G-BA assesses within six months of authorisation whether it adds benefit over an appropriate comparator.

locator.section: The responsibilities of the GBA following AMNOG

covered.statement: The G-BA may hand a medicine's benefit assessment to the Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG) or other third parties.
The G-BA's resolution on a new medicine sets out the extent of added benefit, which patient groups qualify, quality requirements for its use and the cost of treatment.

locator.section: Consultation and decision-making in the GBA

covered.statement: The national association of sickness funds and the manufacturer then have six months to agree the price statutory insurance pays, as a rebate on the launch price; if they fail, an arbitration board sets it with European prices as the yardstick.

A new medicine found to add no benefit over its comparator joins the reference price system within six months of launch; if no reference group fits, a price is agreed, and its annual treatment cost may not exceed the comparator's.
A statutory insurance finance law passed in November 2022 (GKV-FinStG) aimed to cut statutory insurers' drug spending and changed the AMNOG price negotiations in several ways.

Under the 2022 law, the period of free pricing after launch was cut from 12 to six months; afterwards, drugs with minor or non-quantifiable added benefit are priced no higher than their comparator, and those with no added benefit 10% below it.

cost_sharing.statement: Out-of-pocket payments made up 11% of health spending in 2023, below the EU average of 16%.
Outpatient prescriptions carry a 10% co-payment of at least EUR 5 and at most EUR 10; under-18s are exempt.
Total co-payments are capped as a share of income, with a lower cap for people with chronic conditions, but patients must apply for the cap, which may limit its use.
Dental care carries explicit cost sharing because statutory insurance does not fully cover it, so many people rely on supplementary insurance.
In 2022, 38% of out-of-pocket spending went on long-term care, the largest category, because statutory long-term care insurance pays only part of the cost.

financial_hardship.statement: Among people who sought help from a debt counselling service in 2025, illness, addiction or accident was the most often named main trigger of over-indebtedness (18%), ahead of unemployment (about 17%).
Just over half of the people counselled in 2025 lived alone, and for about 24% of them health problems were the main trigger of their over-indebtedness.

locator.section: Mehrheit der beratenen Personen lebt allein

financial_hardship.statement: The 2025 over-indebtedness statistics draw on 738 of roughly 1,360 debt and insolvency counselling services, covering about 187,000 people; participation is voluntary, and the statistical office warns the figures say nothing about the total number of over-indebted people.

In a multicentre cohort of 1,103 sarcoma patients treated at 39 German centres, 44.7% reported financial toxicity, and their odds of reporting financial difficulties were 2.5 times those of an age- and sex-matched norm population.
In the same sarcoma cohort, patients on a disability pension, on sick leave or holding a disability pass had significantly higher odds of financial toxicity.
Of 100 patients surveyed at the end of radiotherapy at two German centres, 68% reported direct costs, 25% lost income and 31% reported subjective financial distress.

Just under 1% of people with private health insurance were in the emergency tariff (Notlagentarif), which the insurers' association describes as a social tariff that makes premium arrears easier to pay off.

additional_care.statement: Voluntary complementary and supplementary insurance plays a small role, funding about 3% of health spending.
Fifty-two companies sell private health insurance.

access.statement: Of people who needed care in 2024, 1.2% went without a medical examination because of cost, distance or waiting time, against 3.6% across the EU.
Among people needing dental care, 0.9% reported unmet needs in 2024, the second-lowest share in the EU (average 6.3%).
Unmet need for mental health care among adults rose from 4% in 2021 to 10% in 2024, and too few outpatient psychotherapists are available to meet growing demand.
Almost 15% of people cannot reach an emergency department within 15 minutes by car, but access within 30 minutes is possible almost everywhere.
Germany had 4.7 physicians per 1,000 people in 2023, but GPs made up only about 16% of them, below the 20% average across 24 EU countries with data.
Nursing shortages persist in hospitals and long-term care, and the nurse-to-bed ratio in hospitals is relatively low, partly because of the large number of beds.
Germany had 12.3 nurses per 1,000 people in 2023, well above the EU average of 8.5.

outcomes.statement: Life expectancy at birth was 81.5 years in 2024, 0.2 years below the EU average.
Between 2010 and 2019 life expectancy rose by 0.8 years, about half the EU-wide gain of 1.5 years.
In 2022 there were 83 treatable and 165 preventable deaths per 100,000 people, both below EU averages.
After a heart attack, 30-day hospital mortality was 8.6% in 2021, higher than in Denmark (4.8%), the Netherlands (2.9%), Switzerland (5.1%) and Austria (5.8%).

In claims data from one large German insurer comparing 2005-2008, 2009-2012 and 2013-2016, the life-expectancy gap between low- and high-income groups widened among older men, while inequality narrowed slightly among women.
In the GBD 2019 study, Germany's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 87.0 (95% uncertainty interval 84.3-89.2) in 2019, 19.0 points higher than in 1990.

outcomes.statement: By age group in the GBD 2019 study, Germany's 2019 HAQ Index score was 94.7 for ages 0-14, 87.3 for ages 15-64 and 75.4 for ages 65-74.

locator.table: Table: HAQ Index estimates by location; row values in order: 2019 overall (0-74 years), young (0-14), working (15-64), post-working (65-74), then absolute change 1990-2019 for the same four groups

outcomes.statement: In the GBD 2016 study, Germany's HAQ Index score rose from 78.9 in 1990 to 86.1 in 2000 and 92.0 in 2016.

locator.table: Table 2: HAQ Index (95% UI), columns 1990, 2000 and 2016

costs.statement: Germany spent 11.7% of GDP on health in 2023 (EU 10.0%), EUR 5,414 per person adjusted for purchasing power, the highest in the EU.
Public sources fund 86% of health spending, above the EU average of 80%.
Retail spending on medicines was EUR 743 per person in 2023, the highest in the EU (average EUR 510), and 14% of total health spending, slightly above the EU's 13%.
Statutory health insurance spending was expected to rise by almost 7% in 2026 and by less than 3% in 2027.

locator.section: Press release, paragraph after the minister's statement

what_works.statement: The Observatory's assessment is that the system combines good access to services with financial protection for patients.
Among people at risk of poverty who needed care, 1.7% went without in 2024, against 6.0% across the EU.
Generics made up 84% of the volume of medicines paid for by insurers in 2023, the highest share in the EU, though this share has not grown since 2018.

problems.statement: In a 2025 population survey, just over 20% believed statutory and privately insured patients receive the same quality of care, and almost 80% wanted to end the separate private tier; even among the privately insured and supporters of the liberal party, over 60% agreed.

Primary care, specialist care and hospital care are strongly separated, which fragments care, especially without GP gatekeeping; despite two decades of coordination incentives, ambulatory care quality measured by avoidable admissions is only moderate by European standards.
Hospital capacity remains among the EU's highest: 7.7 beds per 1,000 people in 2023 against an EU average of 5.1, second only to Bulgaria.
The Observatory identifies a complex stewardship structure that favours incremental change and hampers reform, and a large inpatient sector that raises efficiency and overcapacity concerns.
Use of electronic health records is low: only 5.1% of people accessed their records online in 2024, reflecting a slow rollout, low awareness among patients and limited participation by doctors.

reforms.statement: A contribution-stabilisation law (GKV-BStabG) is expected to relieve sickness funds by up to EUR 19 billion in 2027, and a finance commission is due to propose structural reforms by the end of 2026.

The hospital reform introduces service groups, assigned by the federal states to hospitals that meet staffing, equipment and department requirements, and adds flat payments for operating costs on top of DRG payments so funding depends less on admission numbers.
The nationwide rollout of the electronic patient record for the statutorily insured began in April 2025, starting with a trial phase in selected pilot regions.
Hybrid DRGs, paying hospitals and outpatient specialists the same for selected procedures, began in early 2024 for a limited set of procedures.
A EUR 50 billion transformation fund for 2026-2035 pays for hospital mergers, closures and conversions into intersectoral care facilities.
The Hospital Care Improvement Act took effect on 1 January 2025.

us_lessons.statement: Comparing the US with other high-income countries, researchers found the US spent roughly twice as much while using care at similar rates; prices of labour and goods, including medicines, and administrative costs drove the difference.
Administrative costs were 8% of US health spending, against 1% to 3% in the comparison countries.
In a Commonwealth Fund comparison of high-income countries, US health spending per person in 2021 was nearly twice that of Germany, the next-highest spender.
